title: SSRF and Server-Side Request Validation
description: Learn how Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) tricks backend servers into making requests to internal services. Implement URL allowlists in .NET and understand the risks of user-controlled URLs.

data.text: Server-Side Request Forgery, or SSRF, is a vulnerability where an attacker tricks a server into making a request to an unintended destination. Because the request comes from the server itself, it bypasses firewalls, IP-based restrictions, and authentication that would normally block the attacker. SSRF is especially dangerous in cloud environments where a single server can reach metadata endpoints, internal databases, and other sensitive services.

SSRF commonly appears in features that fetch URLs provided by users: webhook registrations, PDF generators, link previews, and import tools. If the application passes the user's URL directly to an HTTP client without validation, the attacker can point it at internal addresses like http://169.254.169.254 — the AWS metadata endpoint — or at internal APIs running on private IP ranges.

terms.definition: An attack where the server is tricked into sending an HTTP request to an attacker-controlled or internal destination.
A special IP address (169.254.169.254) that provides cloud instance credentials and configuration to running servers.
A list of approved domains or patterns that a server is permitted to request, blocking everything else.

data.title: Cloud metadata is the crown jewel
data.text: In AWS, GCP, and Azure, the metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254 returns IAM credentials, database passwords, and encryption keys. An SSRF that reaches this endpoint can give an attacker full cloud account access in seconds.

The safest approach is to avoid server-side requests to user-supplied URLs entirely. If you must fetch external URLs, use an explicit allowlist of approved domains. If your application runs in the cloud, ensure the IMDS (Instance Metadata Service) is disabled or restricted at the infrastructure level. Also validate that the resolved IP address is not a private or link-local address before sending the request.

data.text: Client-side JavaScript cannot reach internal IP addresses directly because the browser's Same Origin Policy blocks it. However, if your frontend sends the user-provided URL to your backend API (which then fetches it), the SSRF risk moves to the backend. Always validate and restrict URLs on the server, never trust the frontend to filter them.

items.text: Avoid server-side requests to user-supplied URLs whenever possible.
items.hint: If you need link previews, use a dedicated, isolated service with strict egress controls.

items.text: Use an explicit domain allowlist for any required URL fetching.
items.hint: Never rely on blocklists — attackers can use IP addresses, DNS rebinding, or URL encoding tricks.

items.text: Resolve DNS and check the IP address before making the request.
items.hint: Block private, link-local, and metadata IP ranges (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x, 169.254.x).

items.text: Disable cloud IMDS access at the infrastructure level.
items.hint: AWS IMDSv2, GCP metadata server restrictions, and Azure IMDS policies provide defense-in-depth.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: SSRF tricks backend servers into requesting internal or attacker-controlled destinations.
Cloud metadata endpoints contain credentials that give attackers full account access.
Always validate user-provided URLs with an explicit domain allowlist on the server.
Block private and metadata IP ranges, and use infrastructure-level protections as an extra layer.
data.takeaway: Never let user input decide where your server sends an HTTP request.
